name: Sara Mensah

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, political parties or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side. Your answers are confidential. What fills a working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead rehearsals from the piano for a small opera company, record vocal practice lines and coach four singers. I have a master's degree in music and have been the person younger players call when a scene falls apart for thirty years. I love the moment the cast breathes together before the first note.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How does the company pay fit home?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm 58, my partner drives a delivery van on variable shifts and our children are grown. The company pays below the usual rate for a senior rehearsal lead because its seasons are short, and few other opera groups are near us. We rent and have two weeks of expenses saved. I keep a paper score and diary; I have never used AI.

say: I'd accept **quicker notices** with paid rehearsal time printed beside scenes.
I'd say a **stage singer** still needs a listening pianist.
think: Our **two-week reserve** and variable delivery wages make cancellations a rent risk.
The **short opera season** stays a problem in mild AI.
do: Request **five paid rehearsals** and written cancellation pay; keep four singer sessions.
Use **paper scores** and save fifth of extra cleared service fees after essentials toward one rehearsal fee.
feel: I feel **anxious** about ordinary gaps between opera seasons.
S0.quote: A faster notice does nothing for a fee the opera company does not owe in writing.
fieldNote: Her **senior piano skill** leads singers, yet the short company's low fees and two-week reserve expose rent.
She **never uses AI** and marks a paper score for every rehearsal.

steps.text: Request five paid opera rehearsals and written cancellation fee; keep four singer sessions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company a quicker notice is fine if the paid rehearsal time stays printed beside the scene. A stage singer still needs a pianist who hears a breath.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Two weeks saved and my partner's changing delivery shifts mean an ordinary cancelled rehearsal reaches rent. AI being mostly hype would leave the short opera season as our main worry.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll ask the company for the next five paid rehearsals and a written cancellation fee, and keep my four singer sessions. In the first year of this mild change I'll continue marking the paper score and save one fifth of any extra cleared service fee toward one rehearsal fee only after rent, food and piano travel are paid.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about the old gaps between seasons. A faster notice does nothing for a fee the opera company does not owe in writing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happened at the cold hall?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: One rehearsal was cut when a hall lost heat last winter. The contract paid the cast but not my preparation day.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would your children cover a gap?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, our grown children have rent of their own. I will not put a family loan in my list of paid music calls.

I'd seek **written rates** for preparation and live rehearsal before another season.
think: Guides bring **nearly one-third** of my own pay.
Unpaid **entrance preparation** may remain even if guide sales fall.
do: List **nine guide invoices** and seek separate written recording, preparation and live rates.
Stop **idle room hire** if orders fall; keep paid opera/singers and ask guild to review contracts.
feel: I feel **anxious** about realistic guide-fee cuts against thin savings.
S1.quote: A good contract cannot make an order, but it can keep the live hours honest.
fieldNote: Her **paid preparation** is at risk if generated guides replace recordings but singers still need coaching.
She **declines new AI use** and safeguards cast audio while seeking a guild contract review.

steps.text: List nine guide invoices and request separate written recording/preparation/live rates
Stop spare room hire on idle days if guide orders fall

Keep booked paid opera calls and singer sessions

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the opera manager whether generated vocal practice lines will replace my paid recordings. I'd ask for written preparation and live rehearsal rates before signing another season.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Those vocal lines bring almost a third of my own pay. If singers buy generated guides, the company may still expect me to fix their entrances without paying for that preparation.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll list the last nine vocal-guide invoices and ask the company to separate paid recording, preparation and live rehearsal rates. In the first year, if guide orders fall, I'll stop hiring the spare rehearsal room on idle days, keep booked singer and opera work, and ask the musicians guild to inspect any revised contract before I sign; I won't test a new AI tool with private cast audio.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a realistic loss of guide fees with only two weeks saved. A good contract cannot make an order, but it can keep the live hours honest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try a new AI recording tool?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would only watch a trusted player demonstrate a tool on their own nameless music with paid-use permission and approved storage. I am not buying a trial or giving it a singer's voice.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the guild check?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The guild should check whether the new rate pays preparation before a singer ever enters the room. I can show nine invoices with those hours.

I'd seek **signed live rehearsals** while the company still books us.
think: I expect **nearly one-third pay** from guides to end in 2028.
Further **live opera cuts** remain possible, not certain.
do: Total **guide income**, request signed opera calls and actual pension statements before stopping work.
Seek **posted paid rehearsal coach** after live cuts if master’s/opera leadership qualify and live coaching/preparation pay; require written replacement net after travel/bus.
Keep **rehearsals and singers** until a suitable signed offer.
feel: I feel **alarmed** about expected guide loss with two weeks saved.
S2.quote: A master's degree will not pay the flat rent when a contract ends.
fieldNote: Expected **2028 guide loss** comes before 2031 stage-piano robots; live cuts remain conditional.
A coach move needs **posted qualification**, written replacement net after travel, bus and signed offer.

steps.text: Total guide income; request signed paid opera calls and actual pension statements

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company that thinking AGI by 2028 could make vocal guides before a robot can play stage piano. Playing robots follow around 2031, so I want signed live rehearsal dates now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect guide orders to end in 2028 and remove nearly a third of my pay. Live opera calls may also be cut, but they have not been cancelled from the current season. I lie awake working out which bill could wait after that loss.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll total guide income, ask for signed paid opera calls and request actual pension statements before considering a stop at 60. In the first year after 2028, if paid live calls also fall, I'll seek a posted paid conservatory rehearsal-coach role only if its requirements accept my master's degree and opera leadership, pay live vocal rehearsal coaching and piano preparation, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and the bus works; I'll keep current rehearsals and singers until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed about the expected third of my pay disappearing when two weeks is all we have saved. I can apply to a real role, but there are few similar posts here.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is a rehearsal-coach job posted now?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No conservatory has offered me that role. I would read a current paid posting with actual hours before putting it in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you retire at 60?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never checked the pension amount. A master's degree will not pay the flat rent when a contract ends.

I'd reject **unpriced donation promises** for chapel services.
think: Ordinary software may cut **guide sales before 2031**.
A **chapel service** helps only if it pays and does not displace opera.
do: Seek **separate signed chapel contract** next spring only if fee covers organ playing/prep and bus, written safe room/organ, no displaced work.
Keep **chapel service after 2031** only after guide loss and renewed playing/prep/bus fee and safe room/organ terms without displaced opera.
Keep **current paid opera/singers** and exclude any unsigned chapel wage from budget.
feel: I feel **anxious** about guide loss with a possible paid second source.
S3.quote: A chapel key is not a paid job without a signed rate.
fieldNote: Her **second income** needs a signed playing/preparation fee after bus and written safe chapel room and organ.
She **protects current fees** by refusing any chapel hours that replace opera or singer work.

steps.text: Seek signed chapel service covering own organ playing/prep/bus with written safe room/organ; protect opera/singers
Renew after 2031 guide loss only on same full paid/safe terms without displaced opera

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the chapel that five years to AGI by 2031 gives me time to seek a second paid organ-service contract. Piano-playing robots follow around 2034; I would accept no service on a promise of donations.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ordinary software may cheapen vocal guides before 2031. A separate chapel service could add pay, but it cannot replace opera hours if it clashes with rehearsal days or has no signed fee.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next spring I'll ask a nearby chapel about a separate paid Sunday organ service only if it signs hours and a fee covering my organ playing and preparation after bus fares, and confirms in writing a safe room and playable organ, without replacing booked opera or singer work. In the first year after 2031, if guide sales fall, I'll keep the chapel service only while those paid and travel terms hold and it does not displace opera; if no signed contract appears, I'll keep the current paid calls and not budget an imagined church wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about guide pay fading, though a real second contract would help. A chapel key is not a paid job without a signed rate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Has the chapel offered you work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, the chapel has not offered a service yet. A friend mentioned that it sometimes needs a player, which is not a contract.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make the organ service worthwhile?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The chapel must confirm a safe room and playable organ in writing, and its fee must cover my playing, preparation and bus home. I would not take unpaid 'community' hours and call them a second income.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the company that ten years to AGI by 2036 is time to read pension figures and put live rehearsal fees on paper. Piano-playing robots follow around 2039, but our rent still arrives monthly.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 68 I may still need opera, singer and chapel fees. Two weeks saved now and an unknown pension do not let me name a stopping date.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll request actual pension statements and a written two-year paid opera-call plan, then save ten percent of each extra cleared opera performance fee after rent, food and bus costs toward two months of expenses. In the first year after 2036 I'll keep paid opera and singer work while booked and seek a separate chapel service only with signed playing/preparation fee after bus, written safe room and organ terms and no clash; if live opera pay falls and pension figures leave a gap, I'll seek a posted paid rehearsal-coach role only if my master's and directing experience qualify, paid live vocal coaching and piano preparation remain, and written net pay after travel replaces lost fees and buses fit, keeping current work until a suitable signed offer.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious about a long run of low fees even with time to plan. A pension statement will matter more than a hopeful date in a paper diary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if no extra opera performance pays?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no extra opera performance pays, I save nothing from that source. I won't take rent money to make a reserve target look met.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you seen your pension figures?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, I have not seen our pension statements. I will read the actual amount before leaving any paid singer work.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because vocal-guide pay could end before another rehearsal-lead role opens. Signed opera calls, actual pension figures and a posted qualifying coaching job with written net pay after travel would help.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask who pays the pianist to prepare before a singer arrives. An opera title on a programme cannot buy the next month's rent.

headlineQuote: An opera title on a programme cannot buy the next month's rent.
portrait: Sara is a **58-year-old senior opera pianist** with a music master's degree, partner and grown children.
Her **low pay**, two-week reserve and few nearby senior posts persist despite excellent rehearsal leadership.
She **never uses AI** and seeks written pay for live rehearsal and preparation.
She considers a **separate organ contract** only with signed after-bus pay, safe instrument and no displaced opera calls.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could erase nearly a third of Sara's pay from vocal guides.
whatWouldHelp: **Signed opera calls**, actual pension figures and posted qualifying coaching with written after-travel replacement pay would help.
